prompt: Why must an interrupt service routine send data to a FreeRTOS queue with xQueueSendFromISR instead of the regular xQueueSend?
choices: xQueueSend can attempt to block or trigger scheduling behavior that isn't valid in interrupt context; the FromISR variant is non-blocking and reports whether a higher-priority task was woken instead
xQueueSendFromISR is simply a faster alias for xQueueSend with no functional difference
xQueueSend only works with queues created inside setup(), while FromISR variants work with any queue
ISRs on ESP32 cannot access global variables, so a special function is required to reach the queue at all

prompt: Two tasks run on the same ESP32 core: heartbeatTask at priority 3 toggles an LED every 500 ms via vTaskDelay; workTask at priority 1 runs a tight busy-loop for about 2 seconds before yielding. What happens to the LED's blink timing?
choices: The LED still blinks every ~500 ms on schedule, because the scheduler preempts the lower-priority workTask the instant heartbeatTask's delay expires
The LED blink is delayed by up to ~2 seconds each cycle, because workTask must finish its loop before any other task can run
Both tasks deadlock immediately since FreeRTOS does not allow two tasks pinned to the same core
The LED stops blinking entirely because higher-priority tasks are starved by any running lower-priority task

prompt: Why is it a mistake to call a blocking MQTT publish directly inside the same bare Arduino loop() that also has to sample a sensor on a tight deadline?
choices: Any blocking network call (e.g. a slow TCP retransmit) stalls the entire single-threaded loop, including the time-critical sampling, with no other task able to run in the meantime -- the fix is to give sampling a higher-priority FreeRTOS task and let networking run in a lower-priority task fed by a queue
